Deduction vs credit
Why credits win

lines.say: A thousand-dollar deduction can save just two hundred twenty dollars.

lines.text: A $1,000 credit saves all of it, because each one hits something different.
lines.say: A thousand-dollar credit saves all of it, because each one hits something different.

lines.text: A deduction trims taxable income, so at 22%, $1,000 saves $220 (our math).
lines.say: A deduction trims taxable income, so at twenty-two percent, a thousand saves two hundred twenty, our math.

lines.text: A credit cuts the bill itself, dollar for dollar: the full $1,000.
lines.say: A credit cuts the bill itself, dollar for dollar: the full thousand.

lines.text: Example: the Child Tax Credit, up to $2,200 per child for 2026.
lines.say: Example: the Child Tax Credit, up to twenty-two hundred dollars per child for twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Nonrefundable credits stop when your tax hits $0; refundable ones can pay you the rest.
lines.say: Nonrefundable credits stop when your tax hits zero; refundable ones can pay you the rest.

lines.text: In 2026, up to $1,700 per child is refundable, per the IRS.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-six, up to seventeen hundred per child is refundable, per the IRS.

lines.text: Deductions still help: the single standard deduction grew from $12,950 in 2022 to $16,100 in 2026.
lines.say: Deductions still help: the single standard deduction grew from about thirteen thousand in twenty twenty-two to sixteen thousand one hundred in twenty twenty-six.

post.title: Tax deduction vs tax credit: why $1,000 isn't $1,000
post.ig:
A $1,000 tax deduction can save just $220. A $1,000 credit saves $1,000.
Deductions cut taxable income: in the 22% bracket, $1,000 off = $220 less tax (our math).
Credits cut the tax bill dollar for dollar. Refundable credits can even pay you back.
Tax year 2026: Child Tax Credit up to $2,200 per child, up to $1,700 refundable. Single standard deduction: $16,100.
Sources: IRS tax year 2026 inflation adjustments, Tax Foundation, Kiplinger.
